Final Project: Examining the Relationship Between Demographics, Admission Types, and Clinical Outcomes in New York Inpatients (Niagara County)

Team 2: Simintaj Salehpour,Madeline Bumpus, Nazish Atta, Divya Mistry

December 09, 2025

1 Introduction

Hospital resource utilization and patient outcomes are major priorities for improving the efficiency, equity, and quality of care. Factors such as insurance type, demographics, admission characteristics, and clinical severity influence both length of stay (LOS) and total hospital charges. Understanding these relationships helps identify disparities and supports evidence-based health policy.

Our team focused on differences in LOS across insurance types, particularly Medicare, Medicaid, and Private Insurance. This topic holds personal significance for members of our group who have experienced how insurance coverage affects the timing, quality, and duration of medical care. These experiences motivated us to explore whether insurance type is associated with measurable differences in hospital utilization.

This study provides evidence on the factors that most strongly predict LOS and hospital charges in Niagara County and supports future local health planning and policy decisions.

2 Literature Review

Hospital resource utilization—particularly LOS and total charges—is shaped by demographic, clinical, and financial factors. Numerous studies identify insurance type as a key determinant. Medicaid patients often experience longer stays and higher preventable admissions due to reduced outpatient access (Baseman et al., 2016; Coughlin et al., 2014). Privately insured patients typically have shorter stays and lower average charges, whereas Medicare patients incur higher costs associated with multimorbidity and advanced age (Lochner et al., 2020). Demographic variables including age, race, ethnicity, and comorbidity burden have strong influence on LOS and charges. Older adults and individuals with multiple chronic conditions generate higher utilization, especially for high-burden diseases such as heart failure (Jencks et al., 2009; Dharmarajan et al., 2013; Fonarow et al., 2017). Emergency admissions further elevate costs and prolong hospitalization (Basu et al., 2018). Predictive modeling approaches, particularly regression and machine learning have been applied to estimate hospital charges, with insurance type, age, and severity consistently improving accuracy. Prior studies report RMSE values between $4,000 and $10,000 depending on dataset size and clinical condition (Huang et al., 2021; Friedman et al., 2018). Together, the literature provides a strong foundation for analyzing the Niagara County SPARCS subset and supports focusing on insurance, demographics, and severity as drivers of LOS and charges.

3 Dataset Description

This analysis uses data from the New York State Department of Health (NYSDOH) Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (SPARCS), specifically the Hospital Inpatient Discharges (SPARCS De-Identified) dataset for Niagara County, 2024. The dataset includes detailed records of all hospital discharges statewide, with variables describing patient demographics, diagnoses, procedures, hospital facility characteristics, insurance/payment type, admission type, and clinical outcomes. Each row represents one patient discharge, allowing for analysis of trends in hospital length of stay, cost, and patient mix. The full dataset contains over 2 million records across New York State; for this project, a subset of approximately 6,913 discharges from Niagara County was used to maintain manageability and statistical power. This dataset is publicly available through the NY Open Data Portal and is widely used in healthcare policy, public health, and data science research.

4 Data Preparation

The raw Niagara County SPARCS 2024 dataset required several preprocessing steps to ensure data quality and suitability for analysis: we Converted LOS, Charges, and Costs to numeric types, coerced invalid entries to Nan, then dropped rows missing key features such as LOS, Charges, Costs, Age Group,…. at the end,we checked duplicates

4.1 Load Dataset

# Load CSV file
data <- read.csv("Hospital_Inpatient_Discharges_2024.csv")

#Clean column names to avoid backticks

names(data) <- make.names(names(data))

cat("Dataset dimensions: Rows:", nrow(data), "Columns:", ncol(data), "\n")
## Dataset dimensions: Rows: 6912 Columns: 33
#glimpse(data)

4.2 Check Missing data

  • Report missingness by variable: We check if there is a missing value or not. For each column check the missing value.
# --- 1. Summary of missing values ---
missing_summary <- data %>% summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column(variable)", values_to = "n_missing") %>% arrange(desc(n_missing))

#missing_summary

# --- 2. Visualize missingness per column ---
gg_miss_var(data) + labs(title = "Variables VS Number of Missing Values") +
  theme( plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "darkblue"))

# --- 3. Check if there are any missing values ---
clean_data <- data
if(any(is.na(data))) {
  
  cat("Missing values detected!\n")
  total_missing <- sum(is.na(data))
  total_cells <- nrow(data) * ncol(data)
  
  # Remove rows if missing values are few (<5% of total data)
  if(total_missing / total_cells < 0.05) {
    clean_data <- na.omit(data)
    cat("Rows with missing values removed.\n")
  } 
  else {
    # Impute numeric columns with median
    for(col in names(clean_data)) {
      if(is.numeric(clean_data[[col]])) {          # Check if the column is numeric
          clean_data[[col]][is.na(clean_data[[col]])] <- median(clean_data[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)  
      }
    }
    cat("Missing values in numeric columns replaced with median.\n")
  }
  
} else {
  cat("No missing values detected. Dataset is clean.\n")
}
## No missing values detected. Dataset is clean.

4.3 Remove Duplicates

  • Report Duplicates by row: Check to remove duplicates:
dup_count <- sum(duplicated(clean_data))
cat("Number of duplicate rows:", dup_count, "\n")
## Number of duplicate rows: 1
# Remove duplicates
clean_data <- clean_data %>% distinct()

6 SMART Questions

The team developed the following SMART research questions based on data availability, clinical reasoning, and literature review. These focus on measurable outcomes—length of stay and costs—to analyze healthcare disparities.

  1. What factors significantly increase the likelihood of a longer hospital stay (>3 days)?

  2. What combination of patient demographics, admission type, and comorbidities predicts the lowest hospital charges for Medicaid vs. Private Insurance patients in 2024?

  3. Which combination of patient age group, severity of illness, and payer type predicts the lowest hospital readmission risk?

  4. Which factors predict in-hospital mortality, and how accurately can we classify high-risk patients?

6.1 SMART Question 1

What factors significantly increase the likelihood of a long hospital stay (>3 days)? What factors significantly increase the likelihood of a long hospital stay (>3 days)?

We selected logistic regression because our outcome (whether a patient stayed longer than 3 days) was a binary classification problem. Logistic regression provides interpretable coefficients and odds ratios, which allow us to identify which factors significantly increase the likelihood of a long stay. We also used a random forest classifier as a complementary, non-linear model to check whether more complex interactions or variable importance patterns supported the regression findings. Logistic regression offered better interpretability, while random forest helped validate which predictors mattered most.

Using the model, we can predict a patient’s probability of staying more than 3 days based on characteristics such as:

  • Admission type (e.g., emergency admissions predic longer stays)

  • Severity of illness (higher APR severity levels predict longer LOS)

  • Insurance type (patients with Private Insurance or “Other” tend to have lower odds of long stays compared to Medicaid)

  • Age group (older patients show increased likelihood, though the effect size is smaller)

# What factors increase long LOS (>3 days)?

library(dplyr)
library(caret)
library(broom)
library(ggplot2)
library(randomForest)

# 1. Use the cleaned data 

df <- clean_data %>%
  # Create binary outcome
  mutate(
    LongStay = ifelse(Length.of.Stay > 3, 1, 0),

    # Insurance grouping
    Insurance_Group = case_when(
      Payment.Typology.1 == "Medicare" |
        Payment.Typology.2 == "Medicare" |
        Payment.Typology.3 == "Medicare" ~ "Medicare",

      Payment.Typology.1 == "Medicaid" |
        Payment.Typology.2 == "Medicaid" |
        Payment.Typology.3 == "Medicaid" ~ "Medicaid",

      Payment.Typology.1 %in% c("Blue Cross/Blue Shield", "Private Health Insurance") |
        Payment.Typology.2 %in% c("Blue Cross/Blue Shield", "Private Health Insurance") |
        Payment.Typology.3 %in% c("Blue Cross/Blue Shield", "Private Health Insurance") ~ "Private Insurance",

      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),

    # Convert variables to factors
    LongStay = factor(LongStay, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Short","Long")),
    Insurance_Group = factor(Insurance_Group),
    Age.Group = factor(Age.Group),
    Type.of.Admission = factor(Type.of.Admission),
    APR.Severity.of.Illness.Code = factor(APR.Severity.of.Illness.Code),
    Gender = factor(Gender)
  ) %>%
  select(LongStay, Insurance_Group, Age.Group, Type.of.Admission,
         APR.Severity.of.Illness.Code, Gender) %>%
  na.omit()

cat("Final modeling dataset rows:", nrow(df), "\n")
## Final modeling dataset rows: 6910
# Remove rows with 'Not Available' admission type to avoid new levels in test set
df <- df %>% filter(Type.of.Admission != "Not Available")

# Make sure Length.of.Stay is numeric

  mutate(Length.of.Stay = as.numeric(Length.of.Stay))

# 2. Train/Test Split
set.seed(123)
index <- createDataPartition(df$LongStay, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train <- df[index, ]
test <- df[-index, ]

# 3. Logistic Regression Model
log_model <- glm(
  LongStay ~ Insurance_Group + Age.Group + Type.of.Admission +
    APR.Severity.of.Illness.Code + Gender,
  data = train,
  family = binomial
)

summary(log_model)

# 5. Model Evaluation
pred_prob <- predict(log_model, newdata = test, type = "response")
pred_class <- ifelse(pred_prob > 0.5, "Long", "Short") |> factor(levels = c("Short","Long"))

conf_mat <- confusionMatrix(pred_class, test$LongStay, positive = "Long")

print(conf_mat)

6.2 SMART Question 2

What combination of patient demographics, admission type, and comorbidities predicts the lowest hospital charges for Medicaid vs. Private Insurance patients in 2024? —

Objective Identify the combination of patient demographics, admission type, and comorbidities that best predict the lowest hospital charges for Medicaid and Private Insurance patients in 2024.

Dataset Preparation - Insurances labeled as Medicaid and Private; other types removed (Medicare, self-payment).
- Filtered dataset for analysis: - Rows: 4,650
- Columns: 12 (demographics, admission type, comorbidities, hospital metrics)

library(dplyr)
library(forcats)
library(ggplot2)
library(randomForest)

# Data cleaning
clean_data <- clean_data %>%
  mutate(
    Total.Charges = as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9\\.]", "", Total.Charges)),
    Length.of.Stay = as.numeric(as.character(Length.of.Stay))
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Total.Charges), is.finite(Total.Charges), Total.Charges > 0)



# Filter Insurance types
medicaid_pattern <- "Medicaid|federal/state/local/va"
private_pattern  <- "Blue Cross/Blue Shield|Private Health Insurance|Miscellaneous/Other"

hospital_filtered <- clean_data %>%
  mutate(
    Insurance = case_when(
      if_any(starts_with("Payment.Typology"), ~ str_detect(., medicaid_pattern)) ~ "Medicaid",
      if_any(starts_with("Payment.Typology"), ~ str_detect(., private_pattern))  ~ "Private",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(Insurance %in% c("Medicaid", "Private"))


# Keep relevant columns
columns_to_keep <- c(
  "Age.Group", "Gender","Race", "Length.of.Stay","Type.of.Admission",
  "Emergency.Department.Indicator","APR.Medical.Surgical.Description",
  "APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description","APR.DRG.Code","CCSR.Diagnosis.Description",
  "Insurance","Total.Charges"
)
hospital_final <- hospital_filtered[, columns_to_keep]

# Convert low frequency levels to "Other" and handle NA
factors_to_fix <- c(
  "Age.Group","Gender","Race","Type.of.Admission",
  "Emergency.Department.Indicator","APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description","CCSR.Diagnosis.Description")

for(f in factors_to_fix){
  hospital_final[[f]] <- fct_lump_min(as.factor(hospital_final[[f]]), min = 20, other_level = "Other")
  hospital_final[[f]] <- fct_explicit_na(hospital_final[[f]], na_level = "Other")
}
cat("After labling Insurances as Medicaid and Private and remove other kinds like Medicare and self-payment \nStructure of final filtered dataset with demographics, admission type, and comorbidities variables to predicts the lowest hospital charges for Medicaid vs. Private Insurance: ")
## After labling Insurances as Medicaid and Private and remove other kinds like Medicare and self-payment 
## Structure of final filtered dataset with demographics, admission type, and comorbidities variables to predicts the lowest hospital charges for Medicaid vs. Private Insurance:
glimpse(hospital_final)
## Rows: 4,650
## Columns: 12
## $ Age.Group                           <fct> 50-69, 30-49, 50-69, 0-17, 30-49, …
## $ Gender                              <fct> M, F, F, F, F, F, M, F, F, F, F, F…
## $ Race                                <fct> White, Black/African American, Bla…
## $ Length.of.Stay                      <dbl> 3, 4, 1, 2, 6, 11, 2, 3, 5, 4, 2, …
## $ Type.of.Admission                   <fct> Emergency, Emergency, Emergency, N…
## $ Emergency.Department.Indicator      <fct> Y, Y, N, N, Y, Y, N, N, Y, Y, N, N…
## $ APR.Medical.Surgical.Description    <chr> "Medical", "Medical", "Surgical", …
## $ APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description <fct> Minor, Minor, Minor, Minor, Minor,…
## $ APR.DRG.Code                        <int> 243, 282, 320, 640, 751, 720, 174,…

# Remove rows with any NA in predictors
predictors <- c(
  "Age.Group","Gender","Race","Type.of.Admission","Length.of.Stay",
  "Emergency.Department.Indicator","APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description","CCSR.Diagnosis.Description")
hospital_final <- hospital_final %>% filter(!if_any(all_of(predictors), is.na))


# Train/test split function with safe factor alignment
split_train_test <- function(df, train_ratio = 0.8) {
  set.seed(123)
  n <- nrow(df)
  train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = floor(train_ratio * n))
  train <- df[train_idx, ]
  test  <- df[-train_idx, ]
  
  for(f in names(train)[sapply(train, is.factor)]) {
    test[[f]] <- factor(test[[f]], levels = levels(train[[f]]))
    test[[f]] <- fct_explicit_na(test[[f]], na_level = "Other")
  }
  
  list(train = train, test = test)
}

# Split by Insurance
Medicaid_df <- hospital_final %>% filter(Insurance == "Medicaid")
Private_df  <- hospital_final %>% filter(Insurance == "Private")

medicaid_split <- split_train_test(Medicaid_df)
private_split  <- split_train_test(Private_df)

medicaid_split$train$logCharges <- log(medicaid_split$train$Total.Charges + 1)
medicaid_split$test$logCharges  <- log(medicaid_split$test$Total.Charges + 1)

private_split$train$logCharges <- log(private_split$train$Total.Charges + 1)
private_split$test$logCharges  <- log(private_split$test$Total.Charges + 1)

Random Forest Regression:

We selected Random Forest regression because hospital charges are continuous and may be influenced by complex, non-linear interactions among demographics, admission type, and comorbidities. Random Forest provides variable importance measures and captures non-linear effects. We also used logistic regression on a binary outcome (low charges vs. high charges) to provide interpretable coefficients and evaluate the likelihood of low charges.

top_features <- function(rf_model, n = 5){
  imp <- importance(rf_model)
  imp_df <- data.frame(
    Feature = rownames(imp),
    Importance = imp[, "IncNodePurity"]
  ) %>%
    arrange(desc(Importance))
  head(imp_df$Feature, n)
}

# Feature importance plots
plot_feature_importance <- function(rf_model, title = "Feature Importance") {
  imp <- importance(rf_model)
  imp_df <- data.frame(
    Feature = rownames(imp),
    Importance = imp[, "IncNodePurity"]
  ) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))
  
  ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = reorder(Feature, Importance), y = Importance)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    coord_flip() +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = title, x = "Feature", y = "Importance (IncNodePurity)")
}

# Medicaid

private_split$test$pred_rf  <- predict(rf_private, newdata = private_split$test)

Logistic Regression for Low Charges

We also created a binary outcome LowCharge (charges below the median) and ran logistic regression to assess which factors increase the likelihood of low charges.

library(caret)

# Function to create LowCharge, fit logistic regression, and evaluate

evaluate_lowcharge <- function(df_split, median_value, group_name) {
  
  # Create binary outcome
  df_split$train$LowCharge <- ifelse(df_split$train$Total.Charges <= median_value, 1, 0)
  df_split$test$LowCharge  <- ifelse(df_split$test$Total.Charges <= median_value, 1, 0)
  
  # Fit logistic regression
  logit_model <- glm(LowCharge ~ Age.Group + Gender + Race + Type.of.Admission +
                       Length.of.Stay + Emergency.Department.Indicator +
                       APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description +
                       CCSR.Diagnosis.Description,
                     data = df_split$train, family = binomial)
  
  # Predict on test set
  pred_class <- ifelse(predict(logit_model, newdata = df_split$test, type = "response") > 0.5, 1, 0)
  
  # Confusion matrix
  cm <- confusionMatrix(factor(pred_class), factor(df_split$test$LowCharge), positive="1")
  
  cat("\n---", group_name, "---\n")
  print(cm)
  
  return(list(model = logit_model, confusion = cm))
}

median_medicaid <- median(Medicaid_df$Total.Charges)
median_private  <- median(Private_df$Total.Charges)

result_medicaid <- evaluate_lowcharge(medicaid_split, median_medicaid, "Medicaid")

Logistic Regression (Low-Charge Classification) Logistic regression classified encounters into low-charge vs. high-charge groups using the median charge within each age group. This adjustment controlled natural age-related cost differences. Medicaid models again performed better, with higher accuracy (0.90) and more balanced classification errors. The clear decision boundaries reflect more stable cost behavior within the Medicaid subgroup. Private Insurance models showed lower accuracy (0.78) and more misclassification, consistent with greater dispersion in charges. The GLM results further highlight this: the Medicaid GLM produced stable estimates, while the Private Insurance GLM showed numerical instability (nan values and unusually high deviance), indicating that its charge patterns are less well-captured by standard statistical modeling.

6.3 SMART Question 3

Which combination of patient age group, severity of illness, and payer type predicts the lowest hospital readmission risk? Hospital readmissions are costly and often indicate gaps in patient care. This analysis focuses on understanding which combinations of patient Age, Severity of Illness, and Payer Type are associated with higher readmission risk.

We chose Random Forest as the predictive model because:

  • The outcome variable (Readmission: Yes/No) is binary, suitable for classification.
  • Random Forest can handle categorical variables with multiple levels without needing extensive preprocessing.
  • It captures non-linear interactions between Age, Severity, and Payer Type, which are likely present in hospital readmission patterns.
  • Provides feature importance, helping identify which factors most influence readmission risk.

This combination of exploratory analysis and predictive modeling allows us to both describe patterns in the data and make actionable predictions for patient populations.

# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(caret)
library(ggplot2)
library(randomForest)

data <- clean_data
names(data) <- make.names(names(data))

# 2. ASSIGN COLUMNS BASED ON CSV
age_col     <- "Age.Group"
severity_col<- "APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description"
payer_col   <- "Payment.Typology.1"
# Assuming readmission info is 2 columns before last
readm_col_index <- ncol(data) - 2
data$Readmission_Flag <- data[[readm_col_index]]
readm_col <- "Readmission_Flag"

# Quick check

6.4 SMART Question 4

Which factors predict in-hospital mortality, and how accurately can we classify high-risk patients? 

# --------------------------------------------------
# SMART Question 4:
# Which factors predict in-hospital mortality, and
# how accurately can we classify high-risk patients?

#Goal: The goal was to find out which factors increase a patient’s chance of dying in the hospital and how accurately those high-risk patients can be identified.
# -------------------------------------------------
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(caret)
library(pROC)


set.seed(123)

# 1. Create binary outcome: 1 = died in hospital, 0 = survived
clean_data$Mortality <- ifelse(clean_data$Patient.Disposition == "Expired", 1L, 0L)
#2 missing values
q4_data <- clean_data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(APR.Risk.of.Mortality),
    !is.na(APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description),
    APR.Risk.of.Mortality != "Undetermined",
    APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description != "Undetermined",
    !is.na(Length.of.Stay)
  ) %>%
  select(
    Mortality,
    Age.Group,
    Type.of.Admission,
    Emergency.Department.Indicator,
    APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description,
    APR.Risk.of.Mortality,
    Length.of.Stay
  )

# 3. Set variable types 

q4_data$Mortality      <- as.integer(q4_data$Mortality)
q4_data$MortalityClass <- factor(q4_data$Mortality,
                                 levels = c(0, 1),
                                 labels = c("Survived", "Died"))

q4_data$Age.Group                      <- droplevels(as.factor(q4_data$Age.Group))
q4_data$Type.of.Admission              <- droplevels(as.factor(q4_data$Type.of.Admission))
q4_data$Emergency.Department.Indicator <- droplevels(as.factor(q4_data$Emergency.Department.Indicator))
q4_data$APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description <- droplevels(as.factor(q4_data$APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description))
q4_data$APR.Risk.of.Mortality          <- droplevels(as.factor(q4_data$APR.Risk.of.Mortality))
q4_data$Length.of.Stay                 <- as.numeric(q4_data$Length.of.Stay)


# 4. Train/Test split

index_q4 <- createDataPartition(q4_data$MortalityClass, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_q4 <- q4_data[index_q4, ]
test_q4  <- q4_data[-index_q4, ]

# 5. Logistic regression model

logit_q4 <- glm(
  Mortality ~ Age.Group +
    Type.of.Admission +
    Emergency.Department.Indicator +
    APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description +
    APR.Risk.of.Mortality +
    Length.of.Stay,
  data   = train_q4,
  family = binomial
)

summary(logit_q4)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = Mortality ~ Age.Group + Type.of.Admission + Emergency.Department.Indicator + 
##     APR.Severity.of.Illness.Description + APR.Risk.of.Mortality + 
##     Length.of.Stay, family = binomial, data = train_q4)

# 6. Predicted probabilities on TEST set 

pred_prob <- predict(logit_q4, newdata = test_q4, type = "response")

# 7. ROC curve and AUC 

roc_q4 <- roc(test_q4$Mortality, pred_prob)
auc_q4 <- auc(roc_q4)

plot(roc_q4,
     col  = "#0066CC",
     lwd  = 2,
     main = paste("ROC Curve for In-Hospital Mortality (AUC =",
                  round(auc_q4, 3), ")"))

# 8. Classify "high-risk" patients at cutoff = 0.10

cutoff <- 0.10
pred_class_num <- ifelse(pred_prob >= cutoff, 1L, 0L)
pred_class_fac <- factor(pred_class_num,
                         levels = c(0, 1),
                         labels = c("Survived", "Died"))

# Confusion matrix on test set
conf_mat_q4 <- confusionMatrix(
  pred_class_fac,
  test_q4$MortalityClass,
  positive = "Died"
)

conf_mat_q4

About question 4 Initial exploration of the SPARCS dataset revealed strong associations between patient characteristics and in-hospital mortality. Mortality rates were negligible among patients with “Minor” or “Moderate” APR Risk of Mortality classifications but increased sharply for those in the “Extreme” category, where approximately 25% of patients died. Similar patterns were observed for APR Severity of Illness, where greater severity corresponded with higher mortality rates. Age and admission type also influenced outcomes—patients aged 70 years and above, as well as those admitted on an emergency basis, had higher mortality proportions. These exploratory findings guided the development of a predictive model designed to quantify which variables most strongly influenced patient death during hospitalization.

Model Selection and Methodology: Given that the outcome variable, Mortality, was binary (1 = died; 0 = survived), a logistic regression model was selected for its interpretability and appropriateness for classification problems. Logistic regression also allows for estimation of odds ratios, providing a direct measure of each factor’s contribution to mortality risk.

The model incorporated the following predictors: Age Group Type of Admission Emergency Department Indicator APR Severity of Illness APR Risk of Mortality Length of Stay Before modeling, missing and “Undetermined” values were removed, and variables were correctly coded as categorical or numeric. The dataset was then split into training (70%) and testing (30%) subsets to ensure generalizable results.

Model Results: The fitted model exhibited strong discriminative ability, achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.897. This indicates that in roughly 90% of random patient pairs (one survived, one died), the model correctly assigned a higher predicted probability of death to the patient who actually died.

On the test dataset, the model’s classification performance was as follows: Accuracy: 0.952 Sensitivity (True Positive Rate): 0.396 Specificity (True Negative Rate): 0.965 Positive Predictive Value (PPV): 0.211 Negative Predictive Value (NPV): 0.985 While the model demonstrated high accuracy and specificity, its moderate sensitivity reflected the class imbalance present in the data—only about 2–3% of patients in the dataset died during hospitalization. Nonetheless, the model successfully identified a meaningful subset of patients at elevated risk. Key Predictors and Insights Analysis of the logistic regression coefficients revealed that APR Risk of Mortality and APR Severity of Illness were the most significant predictors of in-hospital mortality. Mortality increased from nearly 0% among “Minor” and “Moderate” risk groups to roughly 25% among “Extreme” cases. Older age (particularly 70 years and above) and emergency or urgent admissions were also associated with higher odds of mortality, although their effects were less pronounced than the clinical severity indicators. Length of Stay demonstrated a weaker association—it was often a reflection of underlying severity rather than a direct cause of increased death rates.

Discussion and Interpretation: The findings align with prior literature emphasizing the predictive value of APR-based risk and severity scores in hospital outcome modeling (Author, Year). The model’s high AUC and strong specificity indicate its potential to aid real-world clinical decision-making. Hospitals could utilize similar models to identify high-risk patients early, allowing for timely interventions and better resource allocation. The moderate sensitivity suggests that although the model performs well overall, some at-risk patients may remain undetected. This limitation is partly due to the rarity of deaths in the dataset. Future research could enhance predictive performance through the inclusion of comorbidity data, vital signs, or other clinical measures, as well as by applying balanced sampling techniques.

Conclusion: This analysis concludes that APR Risk of Mortality and APR Severity of Illness are the dominant predictors of in-hospital mortality. The logistic regression model achieved strong performance (AUC = 0.897), accurately distinguishing between low- and high-risk patients. These results reinforce that data-driven approaches, when applied to clinical data, can effectively translate statistical modeling into actionable insights that support improved patient outcomes.

7 Analysis Results

7.1 SMART Question1:

Our analysis found that admission type is the strongest predictor of long hospital stays. Patients admitted with an Emergency/Urgent label has much higher odds of extended stays, while insurance type played a smaller but still meaningful role. Age, gender, and severity of illness showed little predictive power in the logistic model. Random Forest highlighted similar variables but performed slightly worse overall. Because long stays were relatively rare, both models struggled with sensitivity, yet logistic regression provided clearer, more interpretable results. Overall, admission-related factors, not demographics, best explain who is likely to stay in the hospital longer. -

7.2 SMART Question2:

Based on the feature importance from the Random Forest models and Across both Medicaid and Private Insurance, Length of Stay, CCSR Diagnosis, Type of Admission, and APR Severity of Illness emerge as the most influential predictors of low hospital charges, with the lowest costs consistently linked to Newborn admissions, very short (1–2 day) stays, minor illness severity, and low-complexity diagnoses.

7.3 SMART Question3:

The analysis shows that readmission risk is mainly driven by severity of illness, age, and payer type. Patients with higher severity levels and older age groups have notably higher readmission rates. Medicare and Medicaid patients also show increased risk compared to commercial payers. The model and visualizations consistently support these patterns. Overall, focusing follow-up care and support on high-severity, older, and publicly insured patients may help reduce avoidable readmissions. -

7.4 SMART Question4:

In-hospital mortality was rare (~2–3%), so accuracy alone is not very informative. The model showed high specificity and NPV, meaning it reliably identified patients who survived while still detecting a meaningful portion of true deaths. APR Risk of Mortality and APR Severity of Illness were by far the strongest predictors—mortality rose from nearly 0% in Minor/Moderate risk groups to ~5% in Major risk and ~25% in Extreme risk categories. Older age (70+), and emergency or urgent admissions also increased mortality risk but to a lesser extent. Overall, clinical severity and APR risk scores drive mortality outcomes, and the logistic model provides a solid framework for distinguishing high-risk from low-risk patients. -
